Practicing within a theoretical framework and treatment methodology that have vastly expanded the efficacy of talk therapy first imagined by Freud, modern analysts have historically embraced working with difficult patients.

In “When the Body Does the Talking,” Rory Rothman describes the challenges encountered and insights gained in working with somatizing patients over a long-term course of treatment. Case studies are presented, each unique in regard to symptoms, but all revealing unmentalized instinctual conflicts enacted through the body and provoking negative countertransference experiences such as numbness, anxiety, and the feeling of being invaded.

Using Hyman Spotnitz's and Phyllis Meadow's contributions as a clinical and philosophical basis from which to conduct treatment, Rothman has built a theoretical framework to further understand her cases by investigating the writings of (among others) Eugenio Gaddini, Joyce MacDougall, and Andre Green, all of whom emphasize the drives and early mental states, as well as the work of Pierre Marty and the Paris School of Psychosomatics.

Jane Snyder   Developmental psychologist and certified psychoanalyst. She is president of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis where she is an active faculty member and co-directs the Research Committee. She has written and presented on numerous clinical topics and practices in Brookline, MA.

Psychoanalytic case study research is a difficult process. It evokes and repeats feelings, unconscious strivings, and enactments experienced with the patient, as well as conflicts and feelings about research and writing endemic to the researcher. When working with very regressed, preverbal patients, patients on the primitive edge, the researcher may find the experience difficult to endure. Many students get bogged down in this process and have trouble developing a research question or carrying out the data analysis. Examples are given of how to utilize transference and countertransference dynamics to formulate a question that investigates the patient's core conflict.

It is not the usual practice for a book review to be written by someone well known to the author of the book being reviewed. A book review being written by an acolyte or protege of the author is undoubtedly rarer. Therefore, I should state at the outset that I have known Arnold Bernstein as a teacher and supervisor for more than two decades and, moreover, that my bias toward him—my transference—is clearly of a nature that would render it virtually impossible for me to find fault with this book. It encompasses some 17 pieces Bernstein has contributed to various journals during a career in psychoanalysis spanning six decades, and it explores and elucidates a wide variety of topics in the philosophy and technique of psychotherapy, from the most fundamental to the most esoteric. Bernstein synopsizes his design: “My intention is to stimulate some new thoughts by looking at some old ideas and placing them in a new context. In each instance, although the words and ideas are familiar, I hope that by reframing them in a larger context they will acquire fresh meanings” (p. 201).

Indeed, the first two chapters serve as an orientation to psychotherapy and psychoanalysis—not only for those new to the field, but to practitioners seeking a deeper understanding of their practice.

Nigel Mackay PHD

Northfields Avenue
Wollongong, New South Wales

nmackay@uow.edu.au

Nigel Mackay   Associate professor of psychology at the University of Wollongong, Australia. He is the author of the monograph Motivation and Explanation, on Freud's philosophy of science; editor, with Agnes Petocz, of Realism and Psychology: Collected Essays; and author of various papers on psychological theory and method and on psychoanalysis.

A character in Shaw's The Doctor's Dilemma (1911) famously said “all professions are conspiracies against the laity.” Nowhere is this better shown than in the codes of ethics that professional institutions set out. Like mission statements, quality assurance management strategies, promises of service, and the other devices of modern managerialism, they contain sensible, indeed unexceptionable, guides for action. Yet somehow they protect the interests of the institutions, rather than those they ostensibly serve, customers, clients, patients. They defuse complaint and forestall litigation. The idea of professional codes of conduct has so infected modern moral attitude and its expression that they have shifted concern from doing the right and proper thing by a fellow human being to following the appropriate code.

Dilemmas in Search of a Code

Elizabeth Dorsey MSW

Elizabeth Dorsey

1581 Beacon Street
Brookline, MA 02446
dorseye@bgsp.edu

Elizabeth Dorsey   Training and supervising psychoanalyst on the faculty of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, where she chairs the Curriculum Committee. She serves on the editorial board of Modern Psychoanalysis. She has presented on a number of topics, with a focus in recent years on training in psychoanalytic ethics and in clinical ethics for the wider mental health field. She is in private practice in Brookline and Gloucester, MA.

Psychoanalysis has a distinctive ethical quality based on both philosophical and technical principles. The existence of the unconscious and of transference and countertransference determine the analyst's frame of reference and behavior. Working with the intense instinctual pressures of analyst and analysand can strain the limits of the clinician's skills and tolerance. The author considers issues that call most urgently for controls in the consulting room and that reveal the complexities of making clinical decisions: boundary issues; self-disclosure; case selection; transference enactment; extra-analytic contact; informed consent; and end-points of analyses. Case examples highlight some of the dilemmas analysts face when confronted with behaviors that conflict with social mores or laws. The author concludes that the analyst's choices in these difficult situations are guided by consideration of the goals of psychoanalysis and the states of both analysand and analyst with respect to the transference.

Josie Oppenheim

Josie Oppenheim

Josie Oppenheim  

When Freud (1923) described the ego as “deriving from bodily sensations” and as “a mental projection of the surface of the body” (p. 26) could he have been suggesting a new “royal road” to the unconscious? Could the pathways from the body to the psyche and back again be that road? Judging from Psychosomatics Today: A Psychoanalytic Perspective and from the literature this elegant volume is based on, I would say that such a question, demanding a yes or no answer, is not unlike a Zen koan. Devised by the Buddhist patriarchs to entrap the mind of the seeker in a seemingly unanswerable question, a koan, when pondered long and hard, may serve to suddenly eject the mind from its inherent dualism into a profound understanding of the nature of existence, where neither answer and both answers are true.

And indeed the question of whether one can find psychoanalytic meaning in the afflictions of the body can seem imponderable precisely because the patients presenting with somatic ailments described in this literature tend to evince a deafening, psychical silence. Though the surface of their bodies is inflamed with weeping, angry eruptions, nothing seems to roil their mind.

This paper follows the treatment of a woman locked in the grip of an obsessional neurosis. Cut off from awareness of both her love and her murderous impulses, she disables and restricts herself through rituals, fears, and self-punitive behaviors. Bringing her desire and hatred into the transference enabled her to obtain some understanding of her drives and to achieve potential for joy and spontaneity.

Jennifer Andrews MA

Jennifer Andrews

P.O. Box 324
Thetford Center, VT 05075
jenandted@gmail.com

Jennifer Andrews   Graduate of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and is in private practice in Bradford, VT. She works with children and with teachers in the public schools, helping teachers understand how to help their students develop and grow emotionally.

Pivotal moments in the analysis of children occur in surprising and fascinating ways. They are not predictable or measurable, but they create a new feeling in the analyst. The patient expresses something new, and the treatment moves forward. Often the analyst experiences an “aha” feeling, a satisfying feeling that pieces of a puzzle have fallen into place. The patient appears to feel more understood. How do these moments happen? Three case vignettes are presented in which pivotal moments occurred through the analyst's use of induction and countertransference feelings as well as techniques such as joining, mirroring, and contact function.

She is in private practice in Brookline and Gloucester, MA.

The following papers were developed in an ongoing examination, carried out at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, of ethical issues specific to psychoanalysis. The first seminar was conceived of and led by Phyllis Meadow, whose preliminary considerations are presented here in three papers. Faculty and doctoral candidates gathered to consider the particular needs of psychoanalysis in light of existing professional codes and standards. The seminars have continued, with advanced candidates and faculty studying developing trends and problems.

Psychoanalysis has a distinctive ethical quality based on both philosophical and technical principles. The former, the humanistic conviction of the value of truth, personal autonomy, and personal choice, guides the application of the latter. The existence of the unconscious and of transference and countertransference defines the analyst's frame of reference and behavioral imperatives.

The consumer protection movement, the managed-care industry, and well-meaning legislatures have made deep incursions into the practice of the mental health professions, crucially for our considerations in the area of confidentiality.

This paper explores change and stability in nature, including psychoanalytic processes. Mirroring and mutual mirroring are found to be ubiquitous default and survival mechanisms. Mirroring and fractals are allied in that both are characterized as being repetitive in a self-similar manner. The repetitive aspects are related to reenactments in psychotherapy. Chaos theory is seen as congruent with the dynamics of psychoanalytic processes. It is proposed that the structure and growth of fractals found in psychoanalytic processes provide new perspectives on clinical phenomena such as dreams, the repetition compulsion, projective identification, and the transfererence-countertransference matrix.

The author examines ways in which ethical codes are at times misused and the dangers this poses for analysts, patients, and the practice of psychoanalysis itself. Case examples illustrate the use of a code to provide a basis or an excuse for punishment or revenge; as a way of limiting the range of emotions aroused in the analytic session; as an instrument of state control, introducing a third party into the treatment; and as a means of regulating who may practice psychoanalysis and how it is practiced.

Rory Rothman   Training and supervising analyst and faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies and the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. She is a book review editor for the journal Modern Psychoanalysis and a member of the board of trustees of the Society of Modern Psychoanalysts. Her primary research interests involve the psychoanalysis of early mental states and the dynamics of somatization. She is a licensed psychoanalyst in private practice in Greenwich Village and Brooklyn Heights.

The author examines the varieties of somatization and their function in the psychic organization of three long-term psychoanalytic patients. These patients reported extensive use of somatic symptoms, utilizing unique and at times extreme measures in an attempt to maintain a safe and tolerable stimulation level. They all revealed a restriction in their experience of affect and exhibited marked constraint in their free range of thought. André Green's work (1999b) on the place of affect in clinical structures informs the coding scheme devised to study the range of psychic defense mechanisms. For these patients, the body provides protection against threats coming from internal and external sources.

Insights are presented that highlight the underlying early conflicts embodied by these physical symptoms, illuminate the unique transference and treatment issues, and address the potential dangers in working with such cases. Emphasis is placed on the special demands required of the analyst, in particular the extensive use of induced countertransference feelings, a cornerstone of modern psychoanalytic practice.

In seeking appropriate terms of a code of ethics for practitioners of psychoanalysis, the author explores the nature of the transference relationship in detail, in ways that distinguish it from all other human relationships, all the while taking account of the fact that it can and must be understood in the same terms as other relationships. It is found to be a relationship established and sustained in human, as well as in specifically clinical, terms. But for all its unique clinical and therapeutic characteristics, it cannot help but be interconnected with, and responsible to, the surrounding social organization.
